title: GERGELY v. ROMANIA
summary:
In the case of Gergely v. Romania, the applicant, Mrs. Iren Gergely, is a Romanian national of Roma origin who lived in Caşinul Nou, Harghita County. Represented by the European Roma Rights Centre, she brought a case against Romania concerning the violent expulsion and destruction of Roma homes in her community. The harm at the centre of the case was the targeted attack against Roma residents, who faced arson, threats to their lives, and the loss of their homes and belongings, leaving around 150 people homeless and exposing them to severe danger and trauma.

On the evening of 11 August 1990, following rising tensions and accusations against local Roma, a large group of non-Roma villagers gathered, tolled the church bells, and proceeded to burn and destroy Roma houses, including Mrs. Gergely’s. She and her four children fled and hid in a field, witnessing the destruction. Despite immediate complaints and identification of some perpetrators, the authorities failed to conduct a thorough investigation, repeatedly discontinuing proceedings and ultimately blaming the Roma victims for provoking the violence.

The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under several articles, including Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life), Article 13 (right to an effective remedy), and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination). The case was declared admissible, but the judgment does not specify violations or remedies at this stage.

This case is significant as it highlights the persistent vulnerability of Roma and Traveller communities to collective violence and the failure of state authorities to provide protection or justice, reflecting a broader historical pattern of discrimination and impunity in Europe.
